title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
Paper A — Engagement expectations
Gonzalez, M. N., Quartuch, M., & Niemiec, R. (2025). “Stakeholder engagement for Colorado wolf reintroduction: stakeholder-derived metrics of success.” Human Dimensions of Wildlife. https://doi.org/10.1080/10871209.2025.2520848
Paper B — Identity and intergroup conflict
Gonzalez, M. N., Heid, T. N., & Niemiec, R. (2024). “Characterizing social conflict over wolf reintroduction in Colorado: A theoretical model of intergroup conflict.” People and Nature, 6, 2001–2013. https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.10694
Read both full articles. Bring one passage, result, or methodological choice from each that the group should examine closely. Paper A studies expectations of a planning process; Paper B analyzes identity-linked narratives of conflict before the 2020 vote. Neither evaluates ecological impacts of the reintroduction.
Optional extension — Experimental evidence on political identity
Metcalf, A. L., & Angle, J. W. (2026). “Effects of political identity activation and inaccurate metaperceptions on attitudes toward wolves.” Conservation Biology, 40, e70212. https://doi.org/10.1111/cobi.70212
This open-access study reports two randomized experiments with residents of U.S. states with wolves. Read it if you want to compare qualitative accounts of a specific Colorado policy conflict with experimental evidence about when political identity shapes wolf attitudes. It is about wolves broadly, not the Colorado reintroduction process.

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
2 Central question
How should natural-resource agencies respond to identity-linked conflict while designing engagement processes whose influence and limits are explicit?

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
3 What the studies examine
Paper A studies expectations for the Colorado wolf-restoration planning process among highly engaged stakeholders who were not members of the Stakeholder Advisory Group (SAG). It compares their expectations with a research-based engagement-evaluation framework and identifies context-specific criteria and outcomes.
Paper B applies a theoretical model of intergroup conflict to 20 interviews with stakeholders recruited purposively and through snowball sampling before the 2020 vote. It analyzes perceptions of in-group, out-group, intergroup relations, and the nature of the conflict. Its qualitative design characterizes narratives; it does not estimate population prevalence or establish causal effects of identity on voting.
Paper A reports early expectations in a multi-year process. It does not evaluate final engagement outcomes, establish causal effects of engagement, or assess the ecological effects of wolf restoration.

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
4 Discussion sequence — 90 minutes

4.1 1. Opening claim — 8 minutes
Invite each student to offer an initial answer or question. As a class, identify the assumptions behind different answers and note where perspectives diverge.


4.2 2. Set up the case and papers — 12 minutes
Build a compact comparison map together as a whole class; the instructor can record it on the board:

Research questions: What did each study seek to learn?
Population and recruitment: Who was eligible, how were people identified, and who participated?
Data and analysis: How did interviews and each paper’s analytic framework shape the findings?
Inference: What is the strongest claim each design supports?

Use the articles to support each part of the map. Mark details the class cannot resolve from the papers as open questions.


4.3 3. Methods and inference — 18 minutes
Discuss these questions as a whole class:

Paper A invited 345 people to the survey and received 92 responses; 24 people completed interviews. How does recruiting highly engaged external stakeholders shape what it can tell us?
Paper B interviewed 20 stakeholders recruited purposively and by snowball sampling. What kinds of narratives become visible through this strategy, and which are likely missing?
Both use deductive and inductive thematic analysis. How does theory help make identity-linked conflict analyzable? What might the framework obscure?
Paper B sorts stakeholders by position on reintroduction. Does that illuminate meaningful differences, risk flattening within-group variation, or both?
What do the coding procedures establish about analytic dependability? What remains unresolved about validity, transferability, or prevalence?
Which findings are expectations, reported perceptions, or observed outcomes? Where could readers overstate the evidence?
What follow-up or comparative design would help explain how identity, engagement, and management decisions interact over time?



4.4 4. Findings under pressure — 17 minutes
Paper A identifies expectations around representativeness, influence, transparency, independence, learning, conflict resolution, and stakeholder values. It also identifies two stakeholder-derived process criteria—intentional two-way communication and active inclusivity—and two stakeholder-derived outcomes—trust in the agency and support for the final management plan. Paper B finds that strong supporters and opponents often described in-group virtue and out-group failings, while middle-ground interviewees more often described perspective-taking and intergroup relations.
Select one finding for a whole-room close reading. Ground claims in the articles:

Is it a process criterion, a social outcome, or potentially both?
How could an agency operationalize it without reducing it to a weak proxy?
Whose interpretation should count when participants define it differently?
Could pursuing it create a trade-off with another valued criterion?
What evidence would show that the process changed a decision, rather than merely collecting input?
How might identity threat or inaccurate beliefs about the other group shape what an engagement process needs to do?



4.5 5. Whole-room engagement design discussion — 20 minutes
As a class, advise a state wildlife agency planning a contested species restoration. Use both papers to develop an engagement plan that addresses identity-linked conflict and makes decision authority explicit. The instructor records the emerging design, disagreement, and unresolved questions on the board:

Identify the relevant publics and stakeholders, including those not already organized or highly engaged.
Explain how you will address affectedness, representation, access, and Tribal sovereignty where relevant.
State what participants can influence and what remains the agency’s responsibility.
Select two process criteria and two social outcomes to evaluate.
Name one ecological outcome to monitor separately.
Describe how the agency will report what it heard, what changed, and what did not change.
Identify one foreseeable limitation or harm caused by the process itself.

Do not assume that broader participation guarantees agreement, trust, or support.


4.6 6. Compare and critique — 10 minutes
Review the class design. Invite each student to identify its highest-stakes choice or a remaining concern. Challenge the proposal with questions about evidence, legitimacy, feasibility, and unintended consequences.


4.7 7. Closing synthesis — 5 minutes
Complete individually:

“These papers change how I would evaluate engagement by . A remaining uncertainty is .”

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
5 Instructor facilitation notes

Use facilitated whole-room discussion throughout; do not divide students into pairs or teams. With a small seminar, invite multiple rounds of contributions and let students build on or challenge previous comments.
Keep discussion on study design, engagement process, and inference. Students may debate wolf restoration, but ask them to distinguish those normative views from what each study measured.
Preserve the distinction between expectations and outcomes. The interviewees were anticipating how an engagement process should work; this article does not show whether those expectations were met.
Invite disagreement about representation without flattening Tribal Nations into one stakeholder category. Treat sovereignty and governance authority explicitly.
If discussion stalls, ask whether consensus is necessary for legitimacy, whether meaningful influence requires shared decision authority, and how an agency can make non-adoption of public input transparent.
Graduate-level extension: ask students to propose a longitudinal or comparative design that links specific process features to social outcomes while accounting for selection into participation and changing ecological conditions.

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
6 Article limitations worth probing
These are prompts for students to assess, not a substitute for their own critique:

The study focuses on highly engaged stakeholders who were not members of the SAG; it does not represent the Colorado public as a whole.
Interview expectations were measured early in a two-year process and may differ from retrospective assessments.
The sample supports contextual insight, while transfer to other species, regions, and governance settings requires argument.
The article identifies valued criteria and outcomes but does not empirically test which process features produce which outcomes.
Interview transcripts are not publicly available because of the confidentiality commitments made to participants.
Paper B’s 20 interviews characterize stakeholder narratives; purposive and snowball sampling do not support estimates of how common these views are in the public.
Paper B’s pre-vote data describe a specific political moment; they should not be treated as a direct account of current attitudes or post-reintroduction conflict.

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
7 Preparation check
Before class, be able to answer:

What is the unit of analysis in each paper?
How did the authors identify participants?
What is one inductively identified theme, and why is it useful?
What is one claim each paper cannot support?
What additional evidence would you want before advising an agency?

title: Paper Discussion: Identity, Conflict, and Engagement in Wolf Reintroduction
text:
8 Optional extension prompt
Metcalf and Angle report that political identity activation can increase polarization in attitudes toward wolves, while correcting inaccurate in-group metaperceptions can increase positive attitudes across the political spectrum. Discuss:

What does random assignment let the authors infer that the Colorado interview studies cannot?
What remains uncertain when moving from experimental attitudes to voting, participation, management acceptance, or behavior?
How could an agency use this result without treating political identity as a fixed attribute or manipulating participants?

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: The vote set a goal, not an implementation plan
text:
The vote set a goal, not an implementation plan
In 2020, Colorado voters narrowly approved Proposition 114, directing the state to restore gray wolves. Planning followed; the first 10 wolves were released in December 2023.

The mandate set the goal. Managers still had to make the recovery ecologically credible and socially workable.

Time: 3 minutes. This is a 75-minute plan, including transitions. Set up the gap between the voter-approved goal and implementation. Keep this as framing; the first full discussion comes after students have the case and a concrete decision to analyze. Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024); Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024); Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: The management problem has linked parts
text:
The management problem has linked parts

Ecological response: wolf establishment and monitoring
Consequences: who experiences costs, benefits, and risks
Decision process: who influences choices, who decides, and how decisions are explained

Evidence on one dimension cannot stand in for evidence on the others.

Time: 3 minutes. Briefly distinguish ecological response, social consequences, and decision process. Use the three dimensions as a map for the lecture; social evidence complements ecological monitoring, it does not replace it. Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025).


Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Colorado’s decision in time

Gray wolves had been absent from Colorado for nearly 70 years.
Proposition 114 passed in 2020 by 50.9% of the vote.
A multi-year planning process began in 2021; the first 10 wolves were released in December 2023.


Read the papers: Conflict over wolf reintroduction (2024) · Stakeholder engagement success metrics (2025)

The first examines identity-linked conflict narratives before the vote; the second examines stakeholder expectations during planning. Neither measures ecological effects of wolf restoration.

Time: 5 minutes. Place the two studies in the timeline: conflict narratives were studied before the vote; engagement expectations were studied during planning. Neither paper describes current public opinion or evaluates post-release ecological effects. Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024); Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024); Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Diagnose one decision
Consider release timing, conflict-response measures, or monitoring priorities.


For a wolf-release decision, what ecological constraints and affected or rights-bearing perspectives should shape the options, and who has final authority?


Ecological evidence
Affected interests and rights
Decision authority


This is the central Human Dimensions problem: how evidence, interests, and authority meet in a management choice.

Time: 7 minutes. First facilitated whole-room discussion. Give students a minute to identify a release-timing constraint, then compare whose interests or rights should inform options and who makes the final decision. Use the next slides to unpack representation and identity; do not try to resolve every wolf management issue. Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025).


Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Engagement is a management choice
Public information, comment, advisory groups, listening sessions, co-design, and shared authority offer different levels of access and influence.

The key question is not only who can speak, but what they can affect.

Information shared
Options that input can change
Who retains final authority


Time: 4 minutes. Present this as a continuum of access and influence. Note that more intensive participation takes more time and resources and is not automatically the best fit. The class will apply these choices in one focused design discussion. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Who counts, and why?
Claims to representation may rest on different grounds:

Direct exposure to costs or risks
Legal or governing authority
Knowledge, use, or stewardship of place
A broader public interest in wildlife held in trust


No single representative speaks for every member of a community or Nation.

Time: 6 minutes. Briefly distinguish affectedness, descriptive representation, expertise, public trusteeship, rights, and Tribal sovereignty. Note that open applications and online comments may miss people who face access barriers. This slide deepens the decision-diagnosis discussion; do not open a second round here. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Identity shapes how a process is read
text:
Identity shapes how a process is read
Political, rural–urban, occupational, and place-based identities can shape:

Who is seen as a legitimate representative
Whose evidence is trusted
Whether a process feels fair or influential


These identities overlap and vary within groups; they do not determine an individual’s position.

Time: 3 minutes. Connect identity to how people interpret representation, credibility, and fairness. The qualitative study characterizes narratives among purposively selected stakeholders; it does not estimate how common each view is in Colorado. Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024).


Source: Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Political identity is not a fixed proxy for attitude
text:
Political identity is not a fixed proxy for attitude
A recent experiment found that activating political identity increased polarization in attitudes toward wolves; correcting inaccurate beliefs about in-group attitudes increased positive attitudes across the political spectrum.

The experiments concern wolf attitudes in states with wolves, not voting on Colorado Proposition 114 or behavior in this management process.

Time: 4 minutes. Summarize the experimental finding and its inference boundary. Distinguish correcting inaccurate assumptions from manipulating identity; leave extended critique for Thursday’s paper discussion. Source: Metcalf and Angle (2026).


Source: Metcalf and Angle (2026)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: What does a fair process promise?
text:
What does a fair process promise?
A process may aim for representation, transparency, meaningful influence, two-way communication, and active inclusion.

Social outcomes may include learning, trust, reduced conflict, or support for a plan. Participants may judge a process fair while opposing its outcome.

Time: 3 minutes. Distinguish process criteria from social outcomes. Paper A reports stakeholder expectations for transparency, influence, inclusivity, and two-way communication, alongside outcomes such as learning and trust. These were expectations to evaluate, not outcomes already demonstrated. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Discussion: design the decision space
For the wolf plan, consider release timing, conflict prevention, monitoring priorities, or response thresholds.


Choose one decision. Which engagement method fits its timing and stakes, and what level of influence should participants have?


Before options are set?
While recommendations are formed?
After the agency decides?


Time: 12 minutes. Second facilitated whole-room discussion. Allow two minutes to select a decision; spend six minutes recommending and defending an engagement method; use the final four minutes to challenge or revise the level of influence. Keep formal agency authority clear. Let students build on one another’s responses rather than dividing into groups. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Discussion: test a proposed process
Suppose the agency proposes an advisory group, public comment, and local listening sessions for wolf management.


Where is this proposed process most likely to fail for the people it aims to involve?


Who may be unable to take part?
What could make participation costly or unsafe?
How will the agency show how input affected options?
How will it explain a decision that does not follow suggestions?


Time: 6 minutes. Lead a full-room stress test of the proposed process. Trace the path from being invited to having input reach decision-makers and receiving a response. Ask students to name the likeliest failure point and one practical change that would address it. Keep this focused on access and process mechanics; the following slide takes up how to measure influence.

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Measure each link, not just the endpoint
text:
Measure each link, not just the endpoint
For any claimed outcome, specify:

The construct and unit of analysis
Whose perspective is measured
An indicator and time point
A plausible alternative explanation



How would you know whether engagement influenced a management decision?


Participants’ reported sense of influence
Documented changes to options or recommendations
Whose account is included, and when it is measured


Time: 7 minutes. Full-room methods discussion. Compare participants’ reported sense of influence with records of changes to options, recommendations, or decisions. Ask whose account is represented and when to measure it. Distinguish these process indicators from trust and from ecological monitoring; a post-process satisfaction measure alone cannot establish causal impact. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Discussion: what evidence would change your advice?
text:
Discussion: what evidence would change your advice?

For each outcome, what would you advise next, and what evidence is still missing?


Participants report learning but remain opposed to the plan.
Public support rises, but directly affected groups feel excluded.
The process is trusted, but ecological indicators do not improve.


Time: 7 minutes. Facilitate a whole-room discussion across the three scenarios. Ask students to state what additional evidence they would need before recommending a change. Make the connections explicit: social outcomes can affect feasibility and implementation, while ecological outcomes still require ecological evidence. Neither type substitutes for the other.

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Thursday: compare the two Colorado studies
text:
Thursday: compare the two Colorado studies
Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025) examine expectations for stakeholder engagement during planning.

Gonzalez, Heid, and Niemiec (2024) characterize identity-linked conflict narratives before the vote.

One focuses on process expectations; the other on intergroup conflict and perspective-taking.

Time: 4 minutes. Preview the comparison students will develop on Thursday: methods, populations, timing, constructs, and supported inferences. The optional Metcalf and Angle (2026) experiment adds a third method and broader wolf-attitude context. None evaluates ecological effects of the reintroduction. Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025); Metcalf and Angle (2026).


Source: Gonzalez et al. (2024, 2025); Metcalf and Angle (2026)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Reading questions

What can each study claim from its sampling and design?
How do identity and perceived influence appear in the evidence?
What can an agency learn from these findings?
What would require new data?


Time: 3 minutes. Preview Thursday’s paper discussion. Have each student choose one methods question and one management implication to bring to class. The discussion guide uses a whole-room format designed for a small graduate seminar.

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: Close: connect people, decisions, and ecology
text:
Close: connect people, decisions, and ecology

What important question about wolf restoration remains unanswered by these two papers?


Name the decision it affects and the evidence you would need.

Time: 3 minutes. Final round: each student names one unanswered question and the evidence needed to address it. End on the connection among ecological endpoints, social conditions, and management implementation. Total planned class time: 75 minutes, including transitions.

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
section: What evidence would show engagement influenced a decision?
text:
What evidence would show engagement influenced a decision?
Suppose the agency uses an advisory group, public comment, and local listening sessions for wolf management.


What evidence would convince you that stakeholder input influenced a specific management decision?


Who participated, and whose perspectives may be missing?
Participants’ reported sense of influence
Documented changes to options or recommendations
Whose account is measured, when, and what else could explain the change?


Time: 12 minutes. Third facilitated whole-room discussion. Compare participants’ reported influence with records of changes to options, recommendations, or decisions. Ask whose perspective is absent and when evidence should be collected. Distinguish process indicators from trust and ecological monitoring; a satisfaction measure alone cannot establish that engagement changed a decision. Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025).


Source: Gonzalez, Quartuch, and Niemiec (2025)

title: Who Gets to Shape an Ecological Intervention?
text:
Prepare for Thursday’s paper discussion
For Thursday, bring:

One passage or finding from each paper
A note on each study’s sampling, design, and strongest supported inference
One management implication and the evidence still needed to support it


Time: 2 minutes. Preview the preparation task. Students should bring one methods or inference point and one management implication to the paper discussion. The Thursday guide uses a whole-room format for a small graduate seminar.
